shippingNews.postTitle: Duluth Ship Fans Welcome Visiting R/V Neil Armstrong

stories.body: DULUTH, MN – The R/V Neil Armstrong arrived at Duluth Monday morning from its home port of Woods Hole, MA. The University of Minnesota Duluth is working with the research vessel to detect and observe neutrino interactions in Lake Superior. Neutrinos are the most abundant particles that have mass in the universe, and they pass through everything. They are very difficult to detect, so studying them requires special instruments. todayInHistory.title: Life Aboard the Edmund Fitzgerald Described in Letters from Cadet
todayInHistory.text: David "Cowboy" Weiss in 1974. [GLSHS] DETROIT, MI – It wasn't just the hat that earned Edmund Fitzgerald crew member David Weiss his nickname "Cowboy." It was his friend and Great Lakes Maritime Academy classmate David James, who had just watched Frank Zappa's 1971 movie "200 Motels" featuring the character Lonesome Cowboy Burt. When James saw Weiss standing outside a classroom dressed in black and wearing a cowboy hat, the nickname came easily."He looked a little different," James said. Weiss was less "bummy" than the rest of their classmates, who dressed to emulate the sailors they were training to join. The day they met, James gave Weiss his nickname "Cowboy Burt." DuMouchelles auction house in downtown Detroit is selling letters written by a man killed in the Edmund Fitzgerald sinking in Lake Superior on Nov. 10, 1975. The letters were written by David Weiss while he was on the Fitzgerald. The friendship between Weiss and James is chronicled in a series of letters they exchanged while out on the inland seas in 1975, when Weiss was on the Edmund Fitzgerald and James on the Walter A. Sterling. The last was sent Oct. 30, about two weeks before Weiss went down with the Edmund Fitzgerald during a storm in Lake Superior. Twenty-eight crewmates perished along with him. todayInHistory.title: Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest to Speak In Ludington
todayInHistory.text: LUDINGTON, MI – Maritime historian, author and shipwreck explorer Valerie van Heest, whose work has helped shape the visitor experience at all three Mason County Historical Society museums, will be the featured speaker at the society’s annual dinner meeting Thursday, Dec. 3. Maritime Historian Valerie van Heest. [Mason County Historical Society] Van Heest, one of Michigan’s leading maritime historians and shipwreck researchers, will present “History of the Great Lakes,” based on her new book, “A History of the Great Lakes in Twelve Shipwrecks.” The program will explore 250 years of Great Lakes history through a dozen shipwrecks, showing how these underwater discoveries reveal broader stories of conflict, settlement, innovation and change. The annual meeting will take place at the United Methodist Church of Ludington, 5810 Bryant Road. Doors will open at 5:45 p.m., with dinner beginning at 6 p.m. The society’s annual business meeting and organizational updates will follow dinner, and van Heest’s presentation will begin at 7:30 p.m. Van Heest is co-founder and president of the Michigan Shipwreck Research Association and has helped discover about 20 shipwrecks off Michigan’s west coast while participating in archaeological investigations at more than 50 shipwreck sites throughout the Great Lakes. marineWeather.synopsis: This morning, a low pressure of 29.8 inches is Illinois while a high pressure over northern Manitoba high resides at 30.4 inches. By tonight, the low deepens to 29.6 inches south of Lake Erie as the northern Manitoba high expands over the rest of the province. As the low pushes off the New England shore at 29.4 inches Thursday night, high pressure weakens to 30.3 inches over northwestern Ontario. This high slowly settles over Lake Superior through Saturday, still at 30.3 inches. The high expands over the Upper Great Lakes Monday at 30.5 inches and remains overhead through Tuesday.

29.8 inch low pressure will move quickly from the Mississippi River into the Ohio River Valley today, advancing into the northeastern United States on Thursday. Progression of the low will result in steady increases in northerly winds this evening through Thursday, with gusts eventually approaching or exceeding gale thresholds Thursday morning & afternoon as 30.4 inch high pressure builds into the Canadian Great Plains. Best potential for gales will be over the southern two-thirds of the waters, where a Gale Warning remains in effect between 3 AM and 9 PM CST Thursday. Northerly winds will remain steadily breezy---though below gale thresholds---through the day on Friday as the aforementioned high nudges east toward the Hudson Bay. Winds will taper Sunday into Monday as 30.2 inch high pressure builds directly over the open waters. Persistent northerly winds will allow for the development of a band of lake effect precipitation late tonight through Friday. Expecting the band to initially develop over west-central portions of the lake, with a gradual eastward drift Thursday afternoon into Friday. marineWeather.synopsis: High pressure influence gradually exits the central Great Lakes today while the next low pressure system deepens and takes aim at the Ohio Valley. Showers, with potential for mixed precipitation, linger into the weekend as larger scale troughing persists.

A cold front crosses Lake Erie early this evening. Low pressure 29.80 inches tracks south of Lake Erie tonight into Thursday before departing the Mid Atlantic coast by Thursday evening. A trough averaging 30.00 inches will persist across the eastern Great Lakes Friday into the weekend before high pressure 30.30 inches builds overhead from the west Sunday into early next week.

A weak ridge averaging 29.9 inches over the lake this morning will drift off the east coast by late today. A 29.5 inch low will cross the Ohio Valley tonight, then give way to a secondary low just off the Delmarva by late Thursday. This 29.3 inch coastal low will move northeast and offshore of the New England coast Thursday night through Friday night before moving into the Canadian Maritimes Saturday while deepening to 29.1 inches. A 30.4 inch high will then build from the upper Mississippi Valley Sunday to the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley Monday.
